title: How a Cyclone Is Born

endcard.line: Pictures: NASA, ISS crew photographs (public domain). Footage: Mostafameraji (CC0)

segments.say: A tropical cyclone can be hundreds of kilometres wide. And it starts with something as simple as warm sea water.

anim.title: What a cyclone needs
items: Little change in wind with height

segments.say: It needs four things. A sea warmer than about twenty-seven degrees. Distance from the equator, so the Earth's spin can twist the air. Steady winds high up. And a patch of low pressure to begin.

anim.title: The engine
items: Air rises faster; more air rushes in

segments.say: Warm water evaporates. The moist air rises, cools and turns into cloud, releasing heat. That heat makes the air rise faster, and more air rushes in below.
The Earth's spin turns this inflow into a spiral. At the centre is the eye: calm, almost clear, with the strongest winds in the wall around it.
Around India, the Bay of Bengal sees roughly four cyclones for every one in the Arabian Sea. The busy months are April to May, and October to December.
Over land, a cyclone loses its warm water, its fuel, and weakens. But by then the wind, rain and storm surge have hit the coast.
For GS One: warm sea, rising moist air that releases heat, the Earth's spin, and a cyclone that dies once it reaches land.

sources: NCERT Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, ch. 10 (Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems): conditions for tropical cyclones (sea surface above 27°C, Coriolis force, small vertical wind shear, pre-existing low-pressure disturbance); energy from latent heat of condensation; dissipate over land; the eye
IMD, Frequently Asked Questions on Tropical Cyclones: Bay of Bengal sees about four times as many cyclones as the Arabian Sea; peaks in April–May and October–December

quiz.q: Where does a tropical cyclone get its energy?
options: From heat released when water vapour condenses
quiz.why: Rising moist air condenses into cloud and releases latent heat.

quiz.q: Why don't cyclones form right on the equator?
options: The Earth's spin (Coriolis force) is too weak there to twist the air
quiz.why: Without the Coriolis force, the inflowing air doesn't spiral.

options: Bay of Bengal, about four to one
quiz.why: IMD gives roughly four Bay of Bengal cyclones for each Arabian Sea one.

reviewNote: Facts were read against NCERT's chapter on weather systems and IMD's cyclone FAQ. Satellite photos are from the ISS, over open ocean, with no lines drawn. Moving facts: the four-to-one ratio is a long-term average; recent decades show more Arabian Sea cyclones.
